passages.t: Up to Jerusalem: Titus is not made to be circumcised
passages.happening:
“Fourteen years later I went up again to Jerusalem, accompanied by Barnabas. I took Titus along also” (verse 1). Paul went because God showed him he should, “in response to a revelation” (verse 2). He set before the leaders the gospel he preached among the Gentiles. He met them privately, “for fear that I was running or had already run in vain” (verse 2).

The test case was Titus. “Yet not even Titus, who was with me, was compelled to be circumcised, even though he was a Greek” (verse 3).

Some people had pushed for it. Paul calls them “false brothers” who had slipped in “to spy on our freedom in Christ Jesus, in order to enslave us” (verse 4). Paul and Barnabas did not give way to them for a moment, “so that the truth of the gospel would remain with you” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Fourteen years is a long time. Paul counts either from his call or from his first visit to Jerusalem. Either way, he had been preaching for well over a decade before this meeting. His gospel was not new, and it had not been made up to suit the Galatians.

Barnabas was a respected Jewish believer from Cyprus, a Levite (Acts 4:36), who had first brought Paul to the apostles. Titus was a Greek, a Gentile believer who had never been circumcised. Paul took him on purpose. If the leaders in Jerusalem welcomed Titus as a brother without circumcision, the question in Galatia was already answered.

‘Running in vain’ is a picture from the races that every Greek city knew. Paul is not saying he doubted his gospel. He means that if the leaders in Jerusalem rejected his work, the churches he had started would be torn in two, and his years of labour would be wasted.

‘False brothers’ are people who claimed to belong but, in Paul's judgment, did not hold to the gospel. He does not say who they were. ‘Spy on our freedom’ suggests people watching to see whether Jewish believers ate with Gentiles and lived freely with them.

‘The truth of the gospel’ is a phrase Paul will use again in verse 14. For him the gospel has a truth that can be walked away from in practice, not only in words.
passages.ot:
Circumcision was God's sign to Abraham. “This is My covenant with you and your descendants after you, which you are to keep: Every male among you must be circumcised” (Genesis 17:10). That is why the question was so serious. The teachers who wanted Titus circumcised were not inventing a rule. They were reading Genesis.

Paul's answer, here and through the letter, is that God's promise to Abraham came first, when Abraham believed (Genesis 15:6), and that this promise always had the nations in view: “all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:3).

The prophets too had looked ahead to a day when Gentiles would come to God as Gentiles. Isaiah says that foreigners who join themselves to the LORD will be brought to his holy mountain, “for My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations” (Isaiah 56:7).
passages.hard:
How does this visit fit with the story in Acts?

Acts tells of two visits of Paul to Jerusalem with Barnabas: the famine visit of Acts 11:27-30, and the meeting of Acts 15, often called the Jerusalem council. Readers answer in three ways. Many think Galatians 2 is Paul's side of the council of Acts 15: the same people, the same question, the same result. Others think it is the famine visit of Acts 11, because Paul went after a revelation and the leaders asked him to remember the poor; on that view Galatians was written before the council. A third view sees it as a private meeting of its own. The site's notes on Acts 11:27-30 and Acts 15:6-11, and the book page on Galatians, set out each view. These notes do not choose. On every view, the leaders in Jerusalem accepted Titus without circumcision, and that is Paul's point.
passages.asks: Paul took Titus with him so that the question would be answered with a person, not only with an argument. Ask who in your church is welcomed only if they become like everyone else. And notice that Paul, sure of his gospel, still went to Jerusalem to seek agreement. Ask how you hold your convictions: firmly, and still willing to sit down with other believers.

passages.t: The right hand of fellowship, and the poor
passages.happening:
Paul turns to the leaders in Jerusalem, “the highly esteemed” (verse 6). Whatever they were, it made no difference to him, because “God does not show favoritism” (verse 6). They added nothing to his message.

Instead, they saw that God had entrusted Paul with the gospel for the Gentiles, “just as Peter had been to the circumcised” (verse 7). The same God was at work in both (verse 8).

So “James, Cephas, and John—those reputed to be pillars—gave me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, so that we should go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcised” (verse 9). They asked one thing: “They only asked us to remember the poor, the very thing I was eager to do” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Paul's tone toward the Jerusalem leaders can sound cool: ‘whatever they were makes no difference to me’. But listen to what he is doing. He is not belittling them. He is saying that his gospel did not depend on their rank. Then he shows that they agreed with him. That was the strongest thing he could say to the Galatians, who were being told that Jerusalem was on the other side.

Pillars hold up a building. The word was used for leading men, and the church was often pictured as God's temple. James was the Lord's brother, Cephas was Peter, and John was the son of Zebedee, one of the Twelve.

‘The right hand of fellowship’ was a public handshake of agreement and partnership. It meant: we are in this together. There was one gospel, and two fields of work. Peter's work was mainly among Jews, Paul's mainly among Gentiles. It was a division of labour, not two different messages.

‘Remember the poor’ points to the believers in Jerusalem, many of whom were poor. Paul did remember them. For years he gathered a gift from his Gentile churches for them (Romans 15:26; 2 Corinthians 8 and 9). That gift was more than money. It showed that Jewish and Gentile believers were one family.
passages.ot:
‘God does not show favoritism’ is the language of the law. Moses said of God that he is “the great, mighty, and awesome God, showing no partiality and accepting no bribe” (Deuteronomy 10:17). Paul applies it to church leaders: God does not judge the gospel by the rank of those who carry it.

Care for the poor runs through the whole Old Testament. The law told Israel that “there will never cease to be poor in the land; that is why I am commanding you to open wide your hand to your brother and to the poor and needy in your land” (Deuteronomy 15:11). The leaders in Jerusalem asked Paul to keep that command, and he was glad to.
passages.asks: The leaders in Jerusalem did not ask Paul for loyalty or for credit. They asked him to remember the poor. Ask what that says about what matters most in a church's agreements. And ask who ‘the poor’ are whom you are tempted to forget, near you or far away.

passages.happening:
“When Cephas came to Antioch, however, I opposed him to his face, because he stood to be condemned” (verse 11).

Paul explains what happened. Peter used to eat with the Gentile believers. “But when they arrived, he began to draw back and separate himself, for fear of those in the circumcision group” (verse 12). The ‘they’ were “certain men” who “came from James” (verse 12). The other Jewish believers followed Peter, “so that by their hypocrisy even Barnabas was led astray” (verse 13).

So Paul spoke up, in front of everyone. “When I saw that they were not walking in line with the truth of the gospel, I said to Cephas in front of them all, ‘If you, who are a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you compel the Gentiles to live like Jews?’” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Antioch in Syria was a great city, and its church was the first with many Gentile members (Acts 11:19-26). There, Jewish and Gentile believers ate together.

That mattered more than it might seem. In the ancient world, eating together meant belonging together. Many Jews kept the food laws carefully and would not share an ordinary meal with Gentiles. Peter himself once said, “You know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with a foreigner or visit him” (Acts 10:28). But God had shown him otherwise, in the house of the Roman officer Cornelius. So in Antioch Peter ate with Gentile believers, as family.

Then visitors came from Jerusalem, from the circle of James. We do not know exactly what they said, or whether James had sent them with that message. Peter drew back. Paul says he did it out of fear. It may be that Peter feared trouble for the believers in Judea, where Jews who mixed freely with Gentiles could face pressure in those years. It may be that he wanted to keep the peace with fellow Jewish believers whom he loved. Whatever his reasons, the effect was that the Gentile believers were left at a separate table. The message they heard was: you are not quite family unless you become Jews.

That is why Paul calls it hypocrisy, which here means acting a part you do not believe. Peter did not believe Gentiles were unclean. He had said so. But his actions said otherwise. And because Peter was so respected, others followed him, even Barnabas, Paul's own partner.

Paul spoke ‘to his face’ and ‘in front of them all’. The wrong was public, and so the correction was too.
passages.ot:
The law itself told Israel to speak honestly to a brother who does wrong: “You must not harbor hatred against your brother in your heart. Directly rebuke your neighbor, so that you will not incur guilt on account of him” (Leviticus 19:17).

Proverbs says the same in a sentence: “The wounds of a friend are faithful, but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful” (Proverbs 27:6).

The best-known rebuke in the Old Testament is Nathan's to King David, a great leader who had done wrong. Nathan said to David, “You are that man!” (2 Samuel 12:7). Like Nathan, Paul spoke to a leader he respected, because the truth mattered more than the leader's standing.
passages.hard:
How should we think of Peter here?

Not with contempt. Peter was an apostle who had walked with Jesus, who had preached at Pentecost, and who had first opened the door to Gentiles in the house of Cornelius (Acts 10). He would later stand up in Jerusalem and say of the Gentiles, “we believe it is through the grace of the Lord Jesus that we are saved, just as they are” (Acts 15:11). What happened in Antioch was a moment of fear in a good man, under real pressure, trying perhaps to keep faith with people on both sides. Paul does not say Peter had changed his beliefs. He says Peter's actions did not match them.

Paul's rebuke was sharp, but it was not the end of the friendship. Paul later names Cephas warmly beside himself and Apollos (1 Corinthians 3:22), and counts him among the first witnesses of the risen Lord (1 Corinthians 15:5). And a letter that bears Peter's name speaks of “our beloved brother Paul” (2 Peter 3:15). We are not told how the quarrel ended. We are told that both men kept serving the same Lord.

The story is in the Bible not to shame Peter but to warn every believer. If Peter could give way to fear, so can we. Most people who leave others at a separate table do not mean to deny the gospel. They are afraid of what their own side will think. That is the danger Paul names: not a wrong belief spoken aloud, but a wrong belief acted out.

And the dispute was among Jewish believers in Jesus. Peter, Paul, Barnabas and the men from James were all Jews. This is not a story of Christians against Jews. It is a story about how the one family of God eats together.
passages.asks: Peter knew the truth and still drew back, because he was afraid of what others would think. Ask where fear of your own group keeps you from sitting with people Christ has welcomed. And if you have to correct another believer, ask whether you can do it the way Paul did, openly, for the sake of the truth and of the people being hurt, not to win.

passages.t: Justified by faith in Christ, and ‘Christ lives in me’
passages.happening:
Paul goes on, speaking as a Jew to fellow Jews. “We who are Jews by birth and not Gentile ‘sinners’” (verse 15) “know that a man is not justified by works of the law, but by faith in Jesus Christ” (verse 16). So even Jewish believers have trusted Christ, to be set right with God by faith and not by the law, “because by works of the law no one will be justified” (verse 16).

Does that make Christ a servant of sin? “Certainly not!” (verse 17). If Paul builds again what he tore down, that would make him the lawbreaker (verse 18).

Then Paul speaks of himself. “For through the law I died to the law so that I might live to God” (verse 19). “I have been crucified with Christ, and I no longer live, but Christ lives in me. The life I live in the body, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave Himself up for me” (verse 20).

“I do not set aside the grace of God. For if righteousness comes through the law, Christ died for nothing” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
Readers are not sure where Paul's words to Peter end. These verses may be what Paul went on to say at Antioch, or Paul may now be speaking to the Galatians. Either way, they bridge his story and his argument.

‘Gentile sinners’ was a common Jewish way of speaking. Gentiles lived outside the law, so they were ‘sinners’ by definition. Paul quotes the saying in order to turn it over. Even Jews who had the law, he says, have had to come to God the same way as Gentiles: by trusting Christ.

‘Justified’ is a word from the law court. A judge justified someone when he declared them in the right. Paul uses it four times in verses 16 and 17. To be justified is to be set right with God, accepted by him.

Verse 17 answers an objection. If Jewish believers eat with Gentiles and leave the law's boundaries behind, someone might say that Christ has made them sinners. Paul says no. The real wrong would be to rebuild the wall he had torn down.

Verse 20 is one of the most personal sentences Paul ever wrote. He does not mean he has stopped being himself. He means that his old life, lived for himself and on his own record, ended when he was joined to Christ in his death. Now Christ lives in him. And he says it in the singular: the Son of God ‘loved me and gave Himself up for me’. The cross is God's love for the whole world, and it is God's love for one person.
passages.ot:
In verse 16 Paul echoes a psalm: “Do not bring Your servant into judgment, for no one alive is righteous before You” (Psalm 143:2). He adds ‘by works of the law’ to make plain what the psalm already implies. If no one is righteous before God on their own record, then no one is set right by keeping the law.

The great example, which Paul will turn to in chapter 3, is Abraham: “Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6).

And the idea of dying in order to live is an old one in Scripture. God promised through Ezekiel to give his people new life from within: “I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:26).
passages.hard:
Verse 16 holds two phrases that Christians read in more than one way. The book page on Galatians, and the book page on Romans, set out both questions more fully.

‘Works of the law.’ The traditional reading, long taught in Protestant churches, takes it to mean everything a person does to obey God's law, done as a way to stand right with God. Paul's point, on this reading, is that no one can earn God's acceptance, so all must receive it as a gift. A second reading, often called the ‘new perspective’ on Paul, takes ‘works of the law’ to mean above all the practices that marked Jews off from other peoples, such as circumcision and the food laws. It points to the setting: Paul has just told of a quarrel about who may eat with whom. On this reading his point is that Gentiles do not have to become Jews to belong to God's people. Each reading has strong defenders, and many readers take something from both. These notes do not choose.

‘Faith in Jesus Christ.’ The Greek can also be read ‘the faithfulness of Jesus Christ’: Christ's own trust in his Father and his obedience to the cross. Those who prefer this reading note that Paul names Christ's self-giving in verse 20. Those who prefer ‘faith in Christ’ point out that the same verse says plainly, ‘we, too, have believed in Christ Jesus’. These notes do not choose. On either reading, Paul teaches both: Christ was faithful for us, and we are to trust him.

What every reading shares is the heart of the verse. No one is set right with God by keeping the law, Jew or Gentile. God sets people right through Christ, as a gift, received by faith. And so Jewish and Gentile believers stand on the same ground, and belong at the same table.
passages.asks: Paul says the Son of God ‘loved me and gave Himself up for me’. Ask whether you have ever said that about yourself, and meant it. Then ask what in your life is still built on your own record, and what it would mean to let it die with Christ. If righteousness came from our own efforts, Paul says, Christ died for nothing.
